page: Amazon Web Services r6a.large is an entry-level memory-optimized instance based on the AWS Nitro hypervisor and powered by an AMD EPYC 7R13 processor running at 3.6 GHz. Utilizing the x86_64 architecture, it provisions 2 dedicated vCPUs on a single physical core via simultaneous multithreading. The hardware features 16.0 GB of DDR4 system memory clocked at 3 GHz, delivering an 8:1 gigabyte-to-vCPU ratio. The configuration includes no bundled local storage, requiring network-attached storage for persistence, and offers a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps without dedicated GPU acceleration.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong single-core compute performance, with single-core stress-ng placing in the top 25% and a Geekbench single-core score of 1643.0. However, total compute throughput remains constrained by the 2-vCPU hardware envelope, resulting in lower-tier Geekbench multi-core scores of 2024.0 and reduced throughput in parallel tasks like Clang software compilation. Uncached large-block memory bandwidth registers at 31.33 GB/sec for reads and 21.46 GB/sec for writes. In application-level benchmarks, the instance delivers 2.28 million operations per second in Redis SET evaluations and 2.87 GB/sec in static web serving.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, r6a.large offers an economical memory profile for workloads that exceed general-purpose RAM ratios but do not justify larger multi-core instances. The primary architectural tradeoff is the single physical core limit, which caps throughput on compute-heavy operations. The instance is suitable for lightweight relational database hosting, Redis or Memcached caching tiers, small-scale ETL processes, and memory-resident background workers.

The configuration delivers 2 dedicated vCPUs derived from a single physical core alongside 16.0 GB of DDR4 memory, establishing an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio. There is no bundled local storage, and baseline network throughput is rated at 1 Gbps with no GPU acceleration. Benchmarking highlights solid single-core computational output, placing in the top 25% for single-core stress-ng tests, though overall throughput is restricted by the low core count, resulting in lower-tier multi-core and database benchmark scores. Given its high RAM density relative to vCPU allocation, the instance provides qualitative cost advantages for memory-intensive yet low-parallelism workloads, such as small caching tiers, lightweight in-memory databases, and modest background processing tasks.
